**Recap:** So far we have covered why the practice of preregistration
came about, and how to do a preregistration. Now we will outline some of
the main challenges and opportunities of preregistration.

![*Credit: Gracia Prum and Malika Ihle for collating comments on the
challenges and opportunities of preregistration from participants from
previous
workshops.*](images/preregistration pros cons wordcloud.png){fig-alt="wordcloud of the pros and cons of preregistration."
fig-align="center" width="704"}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Benefits of preregistration

Now we will consider how benefits and opportunities of preregistration
exist from individual researchers all the way to the wider research
ecosystem.

### Benefits for researchers

**Improved planning and project management:**

- The process of filling out preregistration document helps **identify
  key information** needed at study design stage

- Outlining data collection methods and analysis plans which **reduces
  ambiguity** and **errors** during data analysis stage

::: {.callout-note title="Do you remember?" collapse="true"}
Do you remember the dilemma Max was having? Having a well thought out
analysis plan with a clear decision tree would help mitigate
encountering Max's situation in the future.
:::

**Builds your reputation**

- Transparently show to the wider research community your plans and
  tests

- Signal that you have taken steps to **mitigate** against hindsight and
  confirmation **bias** [@wagenmakersSevenSelfishReasons2016].

**Easier to write up and publish findings**

- Front loading the thinking and planning makes **writing up** results
  and discussion a smoother process

- If you preregister your analytic **code** on **simulated data** the
  results of your confirmatory analyses will be **generated quicker**
  once you have collected and cleaned data

- If preregistration is approved as a registered report during stage 1
  journal peer review, you have **"in-principle acceptance"**

**Visible productivity**

- Publicly sharing outputs that others can **evaluate** beyond a journal
  article (as evaluation of outputs can be influenced by journal
  prestige)

## Benefits for teams

**Clearer involvement of collaborators/project partners**

- Provides opportunities for project partners to discuss and **refine
  plans** before data collection

- Detailed research plans provide **clarity** for project partners,
  which is increasingly important in the era of **large-scale
  collaborations**

## Benefits to wider research ecosystem

**Increase research credibility and bias**

- **Mitigates** against questionable research practices

- Offers more complete reporting and **transparency** of research
  project

- **Reduces publication bias**, as preregistration/registered report is
  available to read (if not embargoed)

**Check thinking**

- Other people reading your findings can **follow your thought process**

- Gain a deeper understanding of a project and make an **informed
  assessment** [@binneyPracticalRoutesPreregistration2025]

::: {.callout-tip title="Reflection point" collapse="true"}
Can you think of other benefits of preregistration in your research
area?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Challenges of preregistration

There remains a number of barriers to the widespread adoption of
preregistration. There are significant challenges present in the current
**research** and **assessment** **culture** (e.g. "publish or perish")
which influences the uptake of preregistration. Researchers have
**different knowledge** and **experience** levels with Open Science
practices that reflect in **attitudes** and **adoption** of
preregistration. This section outlines some of the commonly perceived
barriers and presents some solutions.

## Challenges: time

*"I haven't got time to do a preregistration"*

*Reframing:* front-loaded effort during the planning stage can help
later on during write up and during peer review (remember the benefits
to researchers above)

::: callout-note
## Did you know?

[Peer Community in Registered
Reports](https://rr.peercommunityin.org/PCIRegisteredReports/) is an
initiative where the research community reviews and recommends
registered reports. There is the option to speed up the Stage 1 peer
review of a registered report with the 'scheduled review'
[track](https://rr.peercommunityin.org/help/guide_for_reviewers#h_61998243643551613309672490).
Authors initially submit a one-page “snapshot” instead of a full stage 1
report.
:::

## Challenges: statistical confidence

*"How do I know my planned statistical analysis is the right one?"*

*Strategy:* Simulate random data with the distribution and sample size
of expected real data and run the statistical test planned for the
study. Repeat the statistical test (e.g. 100 x) and check results are
within the false-positive finding rate of 5%. Run a power analysis by
simulating data with the expected effect size for the study and check
model registers effect at least 80% of the time.

::: callout-tip
Take a look at our simulation tutorial
[here](https://lmu-osc.github.io/Introduction-Simulations-in-R/) or a
more beginner friendly guide
[here](https://lmu-osc.github.io/teaching-material-for-novices/open-research-tools/simulations/).
:::

## Challenges: lack of incentives

*"I don't see the point"*

*Counterargument:* aside from individual researcher benefits (increased
reflection, reduced likelihood of systematic errors), journals are
increasingly prioritizing study preregistrations.

::: callout-note
## Find out more

Next time you read a journal article in your field, take a look at the
journal's webpage and see if they accept preregistered studies and if
there are guidelines for publishing registered reports. This information
is usually in the author resources/guidelines section.
:::

## Challenges: overwhelm

*"There is so much that goes into a study registration"*

*Counterargument:* templates and FAQ pages can guide you and if you are
unable to officially register a study, adopting principles of study
preregistration is a good step (e.g. Open Science Buffet approach,
@bergma2023)

## Challenges: lack of support

*"No one in my team knows or cares about study preregistration"*

*Strategy:* Often a reluctance to try out preregistration comes from a
place of lack of familiarity with the process.Sharing resources, and
suggest a group meeting to discuss/learn more about preregistration to
increase familiarity. Reframe preregistration as a creative opportunity
to plan great science! Planning is where the science is, as other
research processes, like data collection can be delegated.

::: callout-note
## Additional resource

Relate to this challenge? See the preregistration [case
study](https://zenodo.org/records/22307709) which provides a number of
strategies.
:::
